entries.note: The protocol frames every message with a `Content-Length` header, and the body is arbitrary UTF-8 — a diagnostic message routinely contains newlines, and can contain the blank line that ends a header block. A reader that splits on newlines therefore works on every message anyone writes a test for and fails on real compiler output. It also has to tolerate a pipe delivering one byte at a time, which is why the buffer is kept across calls rather than parsed per chunk; the test feeds it a byte at a time for that reason.

When a server exits, everything it said is dropped rather than kept until a replacement contradicts it. Keeping them means reporting a file as broken on the authority of a process that is no longer running — and one that may have died precisely because it was confused about that file. An empty list from a restarting server is a true statement about what the workspace currently knows; a stale error is a false one, and the person cannot tell the difference.

The restart is backed off and bounded, and a server that keeps dying is reported instead of restarted forever, because a crash loop that hides itself is indistinguishable from a language with no diagnostics.

Written first as two passes — expand the directory wildcard, then rewrite every remaining star — which is wrong, because the second pass rewrites the star inside what the first pass just produced. `src/**/*.c` stopped matching `src/deep.c`, and the test caught it. Reordering the passes would have worked and would have left the trap in place for the next person; matching the tokens in one alternation cannot have the bug at all. An intermediate version parked the wildcard behind a placeholder, which ended up in the file as a literal NUL byte: invisible in a diff, and worse than what it fixed.
